title: In the hand of God (Wisdom 3:1–9)
hook: the souls of the just are in the hand of God, read at many funerals

segments.voice: Yesterday, Judith told the elders they couldn't put God on a deadline, and walked out the gate. Your line was a widow saved the city. Did you say your honest sentence? Day four hundred forty.

"But the souls of the just are in the hand of God, and the torment of death shall not touch them." It's one of the readings a family may choose for a Catholic funeral, so if you've heard it, it may have been from a lectern, near a coffin, on a hard day. Some people hear it only there, without ever learning where it comes from. It comes from one of the seven books we met this week: the Book of Wisdom, a book that argues with people who think death ends everything.
screen: `READ FROM THE LECTERN.` → `ON A HARD DAY.` → `FROM THE BOOK OF WISDOM.`

segments.voice: Wisdom speaks in the voice of a king who prayed for wisdom, the voice tradition gives to Solomon, though the book never names him. It has come down to us in Greek, and some readers place its writer among the Greek-speaking Jews of Alexandria. Chapter two gives the other side first. It lets the ungodly speak, and they sound very modern. Life is short and then nothing, they say. Let's enjoy ourselves, and if a just man gets in our way and makes us feel bad, let's crush him and see if his God saves him. Then chapter three answers. The souls of the just are in the hand of God. And the Douay goes on: "In the sight of the unwise they seemed to die: and their departure was taken for misery: And their going away from us, for utter destruction: but they are in peace." Seemed. To someone looking from outside, it's the end, a loss, a ruin. But they are in peace. The writer says their hope is full of immortality. God tested them like gold in a furnace, and received them like an offering. And at their visitation, the Douay says, the just shall shine, and run to and fro like sparks among the reeds. Here hope reaches past death in so many words, and you can see why the Church reaches for it at funerals, and on the feasts of martyrs. And the image is plain. A hand. Not a cloud, not a throne, not a distant place. A hand, the way you'd hold something small and precious so nothing can get at it.
screen: `A KING'S VOICE, IN GREEK.` · `THE UNGODLY SPEAK FIRST.` · `THEY SEEMED TO DIE.` · `GOLD IN THE FURNACE, SPARKS IN THE REEDS.` · then, large: `BUT THEY ARE IN PEACE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: remember someone who has died. Settle, and breathe. Let one person come to mind. A grandparent, a friend, a parent, a child, someone whose funeral you remember, or someone whose funeral you missed. Say their name quietly. Picture their hands, if you can remember them. Then picture those hands held in a larger hand, safe, so that nothing can touch them now. If you pray, you can pray for them; Catholics have an old prayer for this that begins eternal rest grant unto them, O Lord. If you don't, just hold their name for a while. The bell holds the time.
Immortality. The hope Wisdom says is full and unshaken for the just who have died: they seemed to die, but they are in peace. Today's word.
Your line: they are in peace. Today, say the name of the person you remembered out loud to someone else, and tell one thing about them. Day four hundred forty.

fork.setup: you're the writer of Wisdom. you've just let the ungodly speak: life is short and then nothing. how do you answer them?
options: agree, and tell people to enjoy life while they can.
say the souls of the just are in the hand of God, and they are in peace.
say nothing; leave the argument there.
fork.reveal: they seemed to die; their going was taken for destruction; but they are in peace. their hope is full of immortality.

original.note: Greek: in the hand of God, the words of Wisdom 3:1 in the Greek text.

trapdoor: what you thought: a funeral reading.
what it means: an answer to people who say death is the end: the just only seemed to die; they are held in God's hand, in peace.
what a scholar hears: a book that comes down in Greek, in a king's voice, stating hope beyond death outright; its phrase 'full of immortality' uses athanasia.

notes: Editor review (2026-10-01): 3:7 now follows the Douay ('sparks among the reeds'), not the KJV's 'stubble', in voice, screen and match; cut the uncited date and place of writing (Alexandria, 'century before Christ') and superlatives ('one of the most often chosen', 'one of the clearest places', 'the simplest image'); hook no longer tells the listener they 'stared at a coffin and tried not to cry'; 'many Catholics use' softened.
Douay-Rheims wording of Wisdom 3:1–3 quoted from memory; please check carefully.
Date and place: Wisdom usually dated to the 1st century BC (some say early 1st century AD), Alexandria. Confirm 'in the century or so before Christ'.
'One of the most often chosen first readings at a Catholic funeral' is a general claim; soften if a Keeper prefers.
Greek 3:1 'δικαίων δὲ ψυχαὶ ἐν χειρὶ θεοῦ'; 3:4 'ἡ ἐλπὶς αὐτῶν ἀθανασίας πλήρης'. Confirm.
Only the opening words of the Requiem aeternam are cited, in description; the prayer is traditional.
Wisdom 3:1–9 at funerals, martyrs' feasts and All Souls' Day: confirm the howItsDone.
